the population should be of such a class and character as will deteriorate rather than elevate the condition of our people and our country at large. It is the feeling of the people of the North-west that we should bring into that country a high class rather than a low class of immigrants. Our western people are convinced that it is in the highest degree necessary for the welfare of this Dominion that there should not be any deterioration in morality and intelligence and In civilization in the settlement of our western territories.
When I took the liberty of placing these views before the House some years ago, the reply was made that we must have settlers, we must have people to cultivate our prairie lands, and if we cannot get them from one class, we must get them from another. In my opinion, that argument was not good then ; but even if it were, it does not exist now. There are desirable people, our equals in every way, in civilization, Intelligence, enterprise and aspirations, pouring into that country by the hundred thousand. We are, therefore, not dependent on picking up settlers wherever we can. We are getting settlers of a most desirable character, and every undesirable settler tends to keep out a desirable one. That is the point of view from which I regard immigration, and I believe it is from that point of view that the majority of the people from the North-west regard it. They do not want to see their institutions deteriorating. They do not want their political or social or municipal life to be placed at the mercy of people who do not understand their benefits or advantages. In any country whose government depends on the popular vote, every voter is a part of the governing body and in bringing people into the North-west, we are introducing people who will have as much to say in the government and the management of the country as we will ; and if the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) thinks it is a good thing for this country that its destinies should be placed in the hands of those whose ideas and aspirations are not the same as ours, I certainly cannot agree with him. I believe in a vigorous immigration policy, such as has been pursued by the government of this country, but I believe that the success of that policy lies in the improved administration of the land and affairs generally in the North-west as make that country desirable for settlement to settlers of a high class. There is no need of depending on the less desirable class of immigration, when we can certainly get the more desirable class. It cannot be any longer a question as between immigration of an undesirable class and no immigration. The country has got beyond that point. It is now a question, as it possibly was not before, as between a less desirable and a more desirable class of immigration.

Something has been said, I understand, about the paying of bounties or commissions to induce immigration. To my mind, if ever there was need for that system, that need has passed. The payment of bounties and commissions has a tendency to bring the less desirable rather than the more desirable class of people. The work of introducing immigration is carried on in many different ways. Some are better than others ; and I would take the liberty of suggesting to the House that there is a certain system being carried on to-day which is in every way desirable, a system which is producing the best possible results and which may very well be enlarged so as to continue these results. I speak of the system which is followed in one case by Mr. Swan-sen, who is especially an agent for the immigration of Scandinavians, more particularly of Swedish people. He is an enthusiast on the subject. His system of work is to go to the colonies of his countrymen in the United States and deal with the people personally and individually, tie does not induce or ask any man to eome whom he does not consider a desirable settler. Then, when he gathers together as large a party as he can handle well, he accompanies them right to the ground where he intends to locate them, he sees them located, takes an interest in them while they are preparing their new homes, and goes back for another party. That may seem a slow process of inducing immigration ; but 1 may tell the House that, as the result of the work of that one man applied in that way, there have been added to the population of the district which I represent some ten or fifteen thousand people, all of a character which does not admit of any question-intelligent, energetic enterprising people, peopu: full of the highest aspirations of civilization. Another gentleman who carries on much the same work, is Mr. Adamson who goes to Scotland, selects his people there, brings them out, places them and goes back for more. What I suggest is that this system of selected immigration be extended and expanded, and be depended upon for the tilling up of our country. That system I claim, coupled with satisfactory administration and with a sound railway policy for the development of our country, will bring as many immigrants as we can handle from year to year, as many as we can assimilate from year to year, as many as can be brought into the country with advantage from year lo year ; and by that system we avoid any question arising from inducing the lame or the halt or the blind, or the mentally or physically or socially unfit.
Different ideas are held and expressed in regard to this great North-west. There is apt to be, on the one hand, an idea that the North-west does not matter, and the immigration that comes in does not matter so long as it goes to the North-west.

Another idea is that the North-west is so great that it does not matter either, for it will be all right in the end. Now the Northwest is a great country; it is a large country ; but it is not a country without limits or without limitations. That country gives great opportunities for the exercise of intelligence, energy and enterprise ; but it does not provide intelligence, or energy, or enterprise. It gives an opportunity for the people who have these qualities, but if the people who have not these qualities till up that country, then we have such a country as that from which they came. But, the North-west, as I said, has its limitations and its limits. It is not so large a country but that it can be filled up. IVe have not before us the prospect of continuously, and everlastingly. and for ever, pouring people into the North-west. It can be filled up, it will be filled up within a moderate period of time. And I say the responsibility rests upon this House and upon the government, upon any government that may be in power, to see that the people who fill up that North-west, who ultimately will dominate the affairs of this country, are of such a character as shall not lower the aspirations that we have or lessen the efforts w.e are putting forth for the improvement and advancement of this great Canada of ours. We spend hundreds of thousands, we spend millions year after year for the purpose of elevating the material, mental, social and political condition of our people ; and is it to be said that from year to year, while we make this effort with'one hand, we should, with the other hand, bring in a class of people who individually or collectively will doubly or trebly increase the task that is set us. Let me inform the House that there are already in the Northwest some very serious social and political questions^ arising from this indiscriminate immigration, which, if they continue to increase will do to this country, in the west and in the east incalculable harm.
Now, as to the possibilities. Mention has been made of a certain class of immigrants who have come, and objection lias been raised particularly to that class ; and I believe the government is being held up to condemnation because of their efforts in bringing in that class of people. There is a mistake, I believe, in that regard, and many of those who are interested in the subject of immigration make that mistake. The government is not bringing in that class of people. It is not putting forth any effort to bring that class. These people are coming in because of the pressure behind and not because of the efforts put forward to draw them. And therein lies our greatest danger. It is because the conditions in the country in which they live are unfavourable, it is because there is continually pressure behind them, the pressure of political sentiment, the pressure of landlordism. the pressure of race and religion, that they are being driven out of that coun
try into this. And we stand at the mercy of these people in their thousands, in their hundreds of thousands, and in their millions at no distant day. This, Mr. Speaker, is not a fancy picture, it is not a dream ; it is a matter of fact. If my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Roche) speaks as an expert as regard to the appearance of these people, I take the liberty of saying that I speak as an expert in regard to the conditions that prevail in the country from which they come, having received the information from their own lips. There are millions of these people who live under conditions which tend to drive them out of their own country. They certainly find the conditions favourable here, and they are coming in in increasing numbers every year, without government assistance or government aid. This is the danger in which we stand, and this is the future of the immigration question which the House should be well aware of and should be prepared to deal with as I believe it will have to be dealt with.
As to the immigration that is coming from the United States, as I said in the beginning, this is the largest immigration we are getting, and is certainly the most desirable foreign immigration we are getting. The only immigration that could be more desirable would be that from the British islands.
I do not speak of the movement of our own people to the North-west, for that is the most desirable of all, and that, I am glad to say, is a movement that is increasing from year to year. It is a pity that it had not started sooner, but thank God it has started at last, and we are getting our own people to settle in our own country. Canada has been the greatest emigration country in the world. We have sent more of our own people into foreign lands within the last thirty years in proportion to our total population, than any other country on earth, not barring Ireland. The fact is we have sent so many of our people into the United States within the last thirty years that of this tremendous immigration that is coming from the States, a very large proportion are our own people coming back, or their descendants. This fact shows to what a tremendous extent our people have gone to the States in previous years. Now I say these people are desirable, take them in the mass, desirable in every way. They are people of intelligence, of energy, of enterprise, of the highest aspiration. They speak the same language, they worship in the same churches, they have the same political ideals, although they have been enjoying different political institutions. Moreover, these people are the strongest objectors to the idea of indiscriminate immigration. They say they have suffered from that in the United States, and they will hold up both hands against such a policy in this country. We, in the west, believe in a vigorous immigra- * tion policy, but we do not believe in a policy

of indiscriminate immigration. A policy ot selected immigration will till the North-west as fast as is good for tlie country, as fast as is good for tlie Nortli-west, as fast as the people can be properly assimilated, and that is the policy we desire to uphold in this House. We cannot have that policy without a satisfactory administration ot public affairs in the North-west, we cannot have it without a satisfactory policy of railway development in the North-west. We have had a satisfactory administration, we are having a policy of railway development. We believe that the North-west, and very soon all Canada, are entering upon an era of progress and prosperity, such as-it is usual to say, was never dreamed of but such as was dreamed of twenty years ago, but was not realized then, for reasons which it is not necessary to mention, but which is being realized uow to the fullest extent of the wildest dreamers of that day. Because of that fact, it is more than ever necessary that there should be a careful selection of the immigration that comes into our country. It is not now so much a matter of bringing them in as it is a matter of saying who we shall accept.

1 entirely agree with the hon. member for Alberta (Air. Oliver) in his protest against indiscriminate immigration into this country, and in the sentiment that public money is practically worse than wasted if it is spent to increase that menace in the North-west. As a matter of fact, I believe it is a position generally conceded, most people will admit, that the immigration of four or five years ago was a decided hindrance, that it was a menace and a danger, and that we are all very glad that it has practically passed away and that the immigration at the present time is coming from better sources, and is of a better quality. At the same time, there is still need for close scrutiny. AVitli the volume of immigration that is now coming into Canada, it seems to me that we should pay more attention to inspection and less attention to agents in the various countries. It must be admitted that where immigrants come in in large numbers, there is a proportion who are physically undesirable, and we are doing our own people an injustice by letting them come in, we are placing burdens upon our own people, we are endangering the health of the community, and in fact, endangering the general public good. Now, Air. Speaker, in proportion to our population we are getting a tremendous immigration, far larger proportionately than that which has gone into the United States, twTo or three times as large. And as they have for years seen the necessity of very careful inspection, it behooves us to institute likewise a very careful inspection. As a matter of fact, we have a greater necessity for closer inspection than they have in the United States; because they have had for some years a policy of inspection, Mr. OLIVER.
and as it has become generally known throughout Europe that it is troublesome and a waste of money for shipping agents to ship undesirables to the United States, the consequence is that a larger proportion will come to this country. Not only that, but a great many come to Canada first, with the expectation of being able to cross over the border into the United States. This has been recognized and attempted to be met, and now if you go to our stations in the interior of the country where railways terminate that connect with the United States, you will find the officials of their Immigration Department parading our platforms, watching every train that leaves for the United States. They are watching for the physically unfit, and when they succeed in stopping them from going into the United States that means that they are left in Canada. If we watched the ports and refused admission to all the undesirables wherever they were detected, that might serve the purpose, but practically that cannot be done. But the United States officials have found that it is not enough lo watch the ports, and so they watch at our railway stations in Canada where lines connect wHli the United States. At a station some distance west of here, I saw two men on tlie platform looking carefully into the train. As the train approaches the border these officers of the United States Immigration Department board the train and communicate with all on board, to find out who have got tickets that have been given to them at a port of entry. If they find these people undesirable, they are advised for their own benefit to stay on this side of the line. Now unless we pay more attention to inspection, we are getting for our money something that we do not want, something that is going to be troublesome. The amouut of money that is now being spent on immigration is very large indeed and .1 think it would be wise' that the outside expenditure should be limited materially, and that more should be done inside in the way of inspection, and more assistance given to these immigrants in placing them on the land.
Now, Air. Speaker, there is the question of the quality of these immigrants. Unfortunately for us, Great Britain has not got a large rural population that we can draw from. The population in the rural districts there is stationary, one that would be hard to influence. In fact all the associations that surround them are such that it is difficult for Canadian agents to induce them to leave the country, and what is worse still, our agents do not pay a great deal of attention to that class. Unfortunately their principal work, heretofore and at present, is in the large cities of the old country.

What I complain of is that although our agents have been- instructed by their superiors, they still continue to do this work, and to still continue to do it openly, and in fact during the last few months they have insulted some of the citizens of this country who have addressed the British public on the subject. I notice as an instance in the Ottawa ' Journal ' of to-night this item, and this is but one example of what has been going on during the last few months :-
Toronto, July 14.-Fifty old country iron moulders and twenty core and pattern makers reached Toronto yesterday to take positions in the Canada foundry at Toronto Junction, where a strike is on. Upon learning the situation they did not go to work, but many of them attended a union meeting and related their experiences. They said they had been engaged on the understanding that there was no trouble, but that there was a great scarcity of moulders in Toronto. The men are unionists. They have been told that they were wanted, that there were large wages going here, that there were not men enough to do the work aud that there was no trouble. The employers, notwithstanding the prosperity of the country have determined to keep wages down to the minimum at which they were previously, and to accomplish that they have been bringing in outside men to do the work. When this was in full swing at the end of last summer, aud seeing the effect it was having on the industrial centres of this country, more especially Winnipeg,, the mechanics there, as represented by the Trades and Labour Council, had a full statement of the case drawn up. They are mostly men who in their time were workmen in England or in some portion of the British Isles. They understand thoroughly the conditions existing in that country as they do in this
country and they sent a full statement of the conditions here to the British press and it was widely published there. It was immediately replied to by our immigration officer in London, Mr. W. T. R. Preston. He contradicted the statement from top to bottom. Here is a man who does not know the conditions that exist at all contradicting men who know all about them. In further proof of this contention it is not out of place to say that the three labour representatives who have signed the manifesto in question to the emigrating' population of Great Britain are to-day living like princes in comparison to their positions prior to their arrival in Western Canada.
That is the letter of Mr. IV. T. R. Preston to the British public coutradictiug the statement sent over by these men who were selected by the workers of Winnipeg to address the British public. This letter was published in the Manchester ' Guardian ' of June 11, I understand. A reply has been sent to it and a very fair reply indeed. I think Mr. Preston should be notified that it is not in the interest of immigration even for him to continue this kind of campaign over there. I understand fully the influences that are at work behind him. Considering the nature of the contest that is going on between employer and employee I think the workmen should not have any interference from the government agent in carrying on their operations. I do not know who is putting it in the newspapers, but it has been appearing in the British newspapers for some months past. It states that it is by the Canadian Labour Bureau, 13 Charing Cross, London, S.W., and what I point out is that that address is practically the address of the Dominion government agent in London. We have obtained immigration from the United States during the last year which is exactly suited for our country, and we have obtained some very good immigrants from Britain, but on the other band we have obtained a very large percentage of immigrants who are 'anxious and determined to settle in the cities. That has rendered the condition in our cities alarming to the man who has to earn his living. In the city of Winnipeg it has had a very detrimental effect, the result being that the wage-earner has now to buy his supplies at increased prices while his wages have not increased. Is it not a fair argument to

say that the workingmen of this country should be taxed to provide funds to keep immigrant agents in large cities in Europe for the purpose of inducing men to come out here to compete with them and to keep down their wages to a minimum. That is really the effect of this kind of policy. I state here on my responsibility, that there has been no scarcity in Canada of skilled mechanic labour. If you want proof of that, here it is. Whenever an article is scarce there is an immediate rise in the price of that article, but there has been no undue rise in the price of labour in this country. Wages have not increased to anvthing like the extent that the cost of living has increased. The very fact that the Postmaster General can find hundreds of people for his service who are willing and anxious to 'hang on to their jobs at $30 and $10 a month is positive proof that wages have not increased. The people who have come to Manitoba and who have settled on the land are heartily welcome, b'ut I say again that the government has no business to spend public money in inducing the mechanic and ordinary city labourer to come to Canada under the impression that wages are so far higher here than in England and that the cost of living is lower. Why, Sir, we had it stated publicly in the papers by Mr. rreston, the Canadian agent, that in the city of Winnipeg the necessaries of life cost far less than they do in Great Britain. That is a most absurd statement and the only reason why he could possibly have made it was. that he thought the people who knew the real truth were not in a position to directly make a contradiction. It is outrageous to induce people to come into Canada by such a statement as that.
I am sure that the Minister of the Interior is well informed of those things I have mentioned, and I trust he will again assure us that our agent in London, and other agents as well, will not only be instructed that they must not give undue colour to the information which they supply intending immigrants, but that they will also be told that they must carry out these instructions. There is no use bringing people out here under false pretenses and having them disillusionized on their arrival. It is a good deal better to tell people that they would have to work when they come here, and that it is safer for them to have some capital even if they are going to a homestead, than it is to'set on foot the cock and bull story of Mr. Preston that all they have to do is to arrive at the nearest port in Canada and that then they are on the high road to prosperity. This gentleman stated that if he had $20,000 be could bring thousands of families out here and that they would at once start out on a prosperous career. That is no kind of story to place before people who when they arrive here will become disgusted and send back reports that will deter others from coming out.

It appears to be always the case that when there is a very large immigration to a country the ordinary precautions are pushed to one side. It is well known, that taking them on the whole, the Barr colonists were perhaps the finest and best class of people who ever came to this country in such numbers, and that they had more money than any similar number of immigrants who ever arrived here. And yet that colony of respectable people who had been well brought up in the old land were crowded together on board ship in a style that was not decent. That is an evidence of how prone transportation companies are, and government officials are for that matter, to break through the ordinary precautions when a large number of people are being handled. If that is the case even with steamship companies who have to conform to board of trade inspection before they leave British ports, is it not much more apt to be the case on this side considering the comparatively small amount of inspection which exists in this country. I claim that unless you are going to spend money to our own detriment, you have got to have some more strict scrutiny of immigrants than you have at the present time.

There seems to be a consensus of opinion on both sides of the House that the great need of the immigration department at present is a more careful discrimination as to the character and the health and the adaptability of the immigrants who come to this country. Some years ago the feeling was very strong that we should fill up the great North-west as rapidly as possible with immigrants, and little thought was taken as to their character, their occupation, or their suitability for employment in Canada. We are now just beginuing to realize the prophetic vision of these statesmen of thirty years ago who projected great enterprises for the opening up of our North-west. Men who foresaw and foretold that the time would come when that country would De opened up to the teeming millions of Europe, and when prospects would be offered to them which they never experienced in the old world. We are only now coming to realize that prophetic vision ; but we are coming to a point in our history when we should pause and consider whether the present management of that department of the government is as wise and prudent as it might be and ought to be. I think, from the evidence that has come out during the discussion this evening on both sides of the House, that it must be conceded that there is room, and vast room, for improvement. We have already had evidence of the -undesirability of bringing out what we may almost call the sweepings of some of the European nationalities, men who are not desirable as citizens in any country in the old world, and whom their fellow-countrymen were quite willing to let
go, no matter where they went to. But now we realize that it is necessary to the future of Canada that we should use more discrimination in regard to the class of men who are to become the future citizens of this country. We spend large sums of money annually for immigration purposes, and the question whether we get value for that money or not is not to be estimated in numbers of immigrants, but it may be estimated quite as much in the character of the class of immigrants we get. If we get a class of people who are undesirable, physically, mentally, from their national proclivities or from any other cause, we are not getting that value which we ought to have. I know that there has been a feeling expressed, and I entirely agree with it, that it is very desirable that we should get immigrants from the British isles, as they will more readily assimilate with the ideas, thoughts and feelings of Canadians.
It has been admitted by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) that there is just one class of immigrants who are superior to them for the great North-west, that is, immigrants from the older provinces of Canada. We lose a large number of young men from our'older provinces annually, and we may expect to lose them. It is necessary, when young men grow up, that they should leave their homes. ' Home-keeping youths have ever homely wits.' And there is a disposition everywhere among Anglo-Saxons to move about and see the world, and see whether they cannot better their condition. That movement will continue, and it is desirable that we should retain in this great Dominion of Canada as much as possible of that class of young men, especially the farming class, from Ontario and Quebec, who wish to move away from their homes and find other homes and prospects. It is very necessary that we should always bear in mind that one of the great dangers of the future of this country is that with our large extent of territory stretching from ocean to ocean there may arise a dissimilarity of Interest or sentiment or aim ; and it is very necessary that we should endeavour as much as possible to infuse into the population of the great North-west some element that will carry with it a national sentiment, a feeling of love for Canada, something that will bind together the different parts of the country far better than telegraph lines, railway lines, commerce or anything else-a bond of kinship and national sentiment which shall tend to hold us together nationally, and give us larger and broader national views. What is it that gives us the greatest trouble with our fiscal policy at the present time ? Is it not the extent of our territory and the divergence of our interests ? We need a larger and a more national outlook, and we need to preserve it in the great North-west. We do not want the feeling to grow up among the people of the North-west that they can be better served by the United States or by



 )
cultivating commercial or fiscal relations with tiie United States. We rather want a national sentiment that will overlook to some extent these considerations, that will look from one end of the country to the other, and will ask what is best on the whole for this great Dominion of Canada. We want to subordinate local and even racial interests to the general interests of the country. These general interests can be served to' some extent by promoting the settlement, of the great North-west with our own young men, especially with the sons of the pioneers of these older provinces of Quebec and Ontario ; and this much I would claim for them, that whatever assistance may be given to any class of immigrants, none deserve more of this country than the sons of the pioneers of those older provinces.
It is also very desirable that we should have a good share-and I am glad to learn that we are obtaining it at present-of the immigration coming from the old country, especially from Great Britain. I know that there is a feeling sometimes expressed that people who come from the cities of Great Britain are not desirable immigrants ; but from my own personal knowledge I can say that men who have come from the city of London, who have been accustomed to indoor work, but who have brought out with them that native intelligence, industry and indomitable perseverance which pertains to our kin, have made a perfect success of farming operations in Canada, though they never were on a farm in their life before.
I had the pleasure of transmitting a few days ago to the Minister of the Interior a letter from a man who only twelve months ago was in a London warehouse, where he said he had to dress like a duke on the salary of a dustman. But he made up his mind that he would come out to Canada, where, if he could not do anything else, he would go on the soil and try to make a living. He was told by one old man that he would soon be back again with his mother or his grandmother. But he describes how he came out and what he had learned within twelve months, and he said he was enjoying life amazingly in the North-west turning up the rich soil of Manitoba and driving a team across the prairie, an occupation which he had never followed before, and where he had found a new vigour, zest and interest in life such as he never experienced before. Men will be successful if they have the energy, the determination and the intelligence necessary, even though they have not been brought up to agricultural pursuits. There is great room for gathering, even from the cities of the old world, men of this class, who are tired of being slaves to indoor duties all their lives, and who will, if they have the opportunity, make a success of agricultural life. I read an extract from a North Cumberland paper only a week or so ago. the ' Penrith Observer,' which is large-

ly circulated in the counties of Northumberland and Westmoreland, about a number of Barr colonists who had returned and who were complaining bitterly of the misrepresentations that had been made to them by the agencies which had induced them to come out, and also of their reception and treatment in Canada.	.	.
I only give the statement for what it is worth, and to show what reports are in circulation in the press of Great Britain. Although the Immigration Department may disclaim responsibility for the treatment of the Barr colonists in Canada, yet the people of the old country will not make any discrimination. They will simply take the reports from their countrymen who went to Canada, and who complained about being overcrowded on the steamers, and of not having been decently treated in the railway transportation across the country, and of being landed into a wilderness without any of the accommodations they had been promised, and will hold the government responsible. I am not imputing any mismanagement or remissness of duty to the department, but I merely point out the necessity of the government taking under its care and supervision every scheme of emigration, whether promoted by Mr. Barr or anybody else, because if there be any grounds for dissatisfaction, the fault will be charged against the Canadian officials and government rather than against the organizers of the emigration scheme. Therefore it is necessary that the government exercise careful supervision even over private colonization schemes, such as the Barr.colony. I need not refer particularly to the statistics compiled and given to the House by the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson). They must convince every one of the necessity of our using much more careful oversight and discrimination in the character of the emigration we are getting. Our country has great resources and possibilities, but its progress and influence in the future will depend not so much on the numbers as on the character of the population. It is the individual qualities of our people which will tell in the formation of our character as a nation, and that greatness and influence which we all desire this Dominion should attain will only be secured by a more careful supervision and discrimination in our immigration policy.

The extent of our country and its wealth producing qualities are so immense that it will take a great many years to populate it at all adequately. ment from the older provinces of Canada to the United States towards western Canada. We are, in the older provinces, not at nil convinced that the exodus has ceased. We have every reason to believe from the large number of unoccupied farms and the large number of strangers whom we see in our towns, because, while the population in the older counties may be about the same as it was, it is made up to a large extent of new people who are coming into these counties, that a large part of the older population is moving into the cities of New England and other parts of the United States. I do not say at all that it would be proper for the government to endeavour to divert the people of Nova Scotia or New Brunswick from these provinces and take them to the west, although I believe that in a great many cases it would lie largely to the interest of the people of these older provinces many of whom are living under conditions which do not at all compare with the conditions under which they could live after having spent four or five years upon
zen of Europe or of England or of Soot-1 the rich, virgin soil of the west ; still, I

maintain there might be with very great advantage an inquiry made by the government, through the Department of the Interior which would enable the government to determine to what extent this movement of population from the eastern portions of Canada to the United States still goes on and enable it to do everything in its power to divert that movement from the United States to tlie North-west Territories. There iji a discrimination against the citizens of the eastern provinces when he proposes to go to the North-west. He finds, that, whereas, the foreigner from Europe or the settler from the Unitel States is welcomed and every facility is put in his way to enable him to go with comfort, ease and cheapness to take up a home in the Northwest, he is treated simply as a person who is perfectly well able to pay his way, and although he is, I think, by far the most desirable settler that can be found anywhere in the world to go into the Northwest lie finds that the transportation system of Canada is such as to discriminate against him. That is certainly not as it should be, but the reverse. It would be a very easy matter, to my mind, if a system of instruction were used to show to those persons who are dissatisfied with their conditions in the older parts of Canada the advantages of our own west; to secure a large proportion of these people and take them to the west. I tlo not know that the whole of them would choose, if a choice were left to them, to settle upon farms, but the men to be found in these older provinces are of the most adaptable character. The very large percentage of the population devotes itself to industrial occupations. The population produces a large percentage of mechanics and although the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) would seem to maintain that there was no need for any more mechanics in the country, it is impossible for me to make myself believe that any country which is increasing in population as fast as Manitoba and the North-west Territories does not present openings for a large increase in the percentage of mechanics. It is perfectly out of the question to suppose for a moment that where you have settled one hundred farmers you will not require ten or twelve men to minister to their wants just as they must be ministered to, because the farmer is a specialist. He is not a man who fills all his wants. His action is confined to the important business of producing as much wheat as he can out of the quarter section, or half section or section, which has been thrown into his hands. There is no country which offers such inducements for the farmer, and there is no country which offers such inducements to the mechanic whose business it is to minister to the wants of the farmer. Any one who travels through the older provinces may see on every hand evidence of a great movement of population. There appears to be a restless instinct in a man
who is born on our eastern seaboard, which leads him to conclude in some fashion that there are prizes to be got by moving from home. It would seem almost as though a more restless population is not to be found in the world than that which occupies the eastern provinces of Canada. So soon as they come to manhood, so soon as they are masters of their trade and get their avocation, they seem to be prone to venture forth into new fields to explore the world and see what prizes are to be gathered. It ia not uncommon, I regret to say, in the county in which I live, and it is the same in many other counties in the eastern provinces-to find farm after farm abandoned by the first settlers and now reverting into a state of wilderness. In these older provinces there is a country to which it would be the greatest possible advantage to Canada to bring in a population who would be content to farm upon these lands. They are not infertile. Although our country does not possess the amazing agricultural wealth of our western prairies it is still a fertile land. In no part of Canada to-day are to he found so many of the comforts and the pleasures and necessities of life, with the church and the school and the neighbour and everything that goes to render life pleasant and agreeable, as you will find in these older provinces. A long time must expire before one can suppose that even the most fertile part of the west can afford .the settler a home in the same fashion that he would have it in the older provinces. There are features in that life which must make it attractive to one who is not a genuine pioneer, who is not prepared to rough it, who is not prepared to put up with a good many discomforts and a great many hours of loneliness in order to achieve success rapidly. There are conditions in these older provinces that would be most inviting to a large number of people who are living upon small holdings in the old country. If we could succeed in bringing upon the deserted farms of Nova Scotia and New' Brunswick, those who are at present living in Ireland and Scotland and England upon, rented lands w'liere they have to pay a large part of their earnings to the landlords, wiiere they have learned that mixed farming to which our country is adapted, w'here they have learned to care for animals and w'here they have not acquired the desire for these huge crops, and these immensely wide fields! of the west, but where they are accustomed to the smaller culture of smaller holdings-if that population could be induced into the eastern provinces to a certain extent, it would be well for Canada. I am afraid that there is a disposition to forget the needs of these older provinces and to devote nearly all the energy of the Immigration Department to the work of peopling the w'est. It is my experience that those who move from Nova Scotia to the west seem to have an ambition to get as far-west as possible. If you talk to a person

in the county of Pictou who is going to the west, he is not satisfied to go to the neighbourhood of Winnipeg; he has the idea to get as far west as he can, and the great desire of most of them is to stop nothing short of Edmonton. That disposition is not only common to those who are moving from the older provinces of Canada, but I think it characterizes the European immigrant as well, and if we could counteract that disposition and persuade a larger proportion of them to settle in the older provinces where they could procure at nominal prices farms which are perfectly capable of supporting a family in great comfort and of giving large returns to an industrious man who knows how to farm, we would be doing our country a great deal of service. It is true that our western friends are anticipating at a very early day the time when the balance of power in this country will be west of the great lakes, and they are reminding us constantly of it in this House. While they are a very fine people and while we would not like to see them disappointed in their aspirations-possibly if we have to have masters in this country we could not desire better than they-yet, I would think that it is very important to maintain the population of the eastern provinces without diminution. While it is desirable to see the west grow up it is just as desirable to see the population kept as large as possible in the eastern provinces. There are features in the west which we have not in the east, and there are features in the east which you cannot have in the west for a long time to come. There is a far more highly organized system of living in the east, which you cannot achieve in the west except by the expenditure of time and money. Therefore it is of the highest importance to Canada that the whole object of government should not be devoted to increase the population of the west, although I admit this to be a most desirable thing. It seems to me that if an effort were made' to induce a large percentage of the immigrants to make their homes in the eastern provinces, Canada would be just as well served as she is at present by directing that tide of immigration to the far west. In speaking of the east I have to include Ontario, because while at one time we, in the maritime provinces, used to speak of Ontario as the west, I find that now when you get to the real west the people there speak of Ontario as the east. There is no question at all but that Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces are now the eastern part of this country. The condition of affairs in the whole east is that labour and population is being drained from it rapidly either into the manufacturing centres or to the virgin lands of the west, and there is an urgent cry in eastern Canada for labour. There is not in Ontario or in any part of the older provinces, anything like the number of men who are necessary to continue Mr. BELL.
that condition of tillage which was formerly the rule. There is an urgent demaud for labour in the older provinces and through sheer want of labour, a great deal of tillage which so largely contributes to the wealth and resources of the country, is being left undone.
The eastern part of Canada to-day is absolutely suffering from want of (labour. That being the case, I must say that while we are willing to do everything in our power to build up the west, we really feel that the government of Canada should not neglect the east, and that some consideration should be given to the demand of the east for more people. I do not know that the government intends to be partial ; but If any one takes up one of the atlases or one of the maps that are being published, he will find that while great prominence is given to the extraordinary, wide and wealthy country of the west, the older provinces are relegated to where they really fill the position that has been described as the shreds and patches of the confederation of Canada. A map has recently been published in which the plotting is done in such a fashion that all that delightful country in which I have my home seems to be moved some hundreds of miles towards the north pole, and is represented as lying away to the north of Winnipeg, Southern Alberta and Assiniboia. It is sim* ly a result of the map-maker's method : instead of putting the centre of the forty-ninth parallel where it ought to be, about Lake Superior, it is placed away west of that, and the consequence is that the eastern provinces are set away up towards the north, which would naturally give one the idea that if he settled in that part of Canada he would be in danger of perishing from frost. Possibly that is an unintentional misrepresentation ; possibly the necessity of utilizing and developing at the earliest date that country upon which we have spent so much money has unintentionally biased the map-maker's mode of thinking and feeling and depicting Canada when it is being presented to the population of Europe, from which we draw our immigrants. While we admit the greatness of the west, and join with those who express the hope to see that western country developed to an extent which will probably in the next fifteen or twenty years be most amazing and gratifying to those who live to see the results, still it seems to me that those of us who come from the east should occasionally raise outvoices in this House and insist on having a certain amount of the attention of the Department of the Interior and of the government devoted to the work of keeping the population of these eastern provinces as much as jiossible at home ; or, if it will not stay at home, diverting it to our own North-| west, and, in place of that population, bring: ing into the older provinces some of the people whom we can get from the British isles or the northern countries of Europe.

Perhaps the most desirable immigration going into the North-west to-day is that from the United States-that overflow, consisting partly of those who were once Canadians and who are coming back from the United States, and partly of those who have gone into Minnesota and Dakota for a time and are now moving into the North-west. That immigration is going into the country at such a rate that the government could probably dispense with some of the expenditure which they are devoting to attracting that immigration. The eastern provinces get none of that overflow, and the immigrants brought into this country from Europe by the machinery and the expenditure of the Dominion government do not stop in the eastern provinces, but are hurried off to the western part of Canada. But. in view of what has been done in some of our provinces in the east, I maintain that we cannot look upon that as a good thing, either for the immigrants themselves or for the country. There can be no doubt that if the Englishmen, Scotchmen, Irishmen, Finlanders or any other men from the northern part of Europe coming to Canada to make it their home, could be induced to spend a number of years in the eastern provinces, to become acclimatized, and to acquire a capacity of making homes for themselves anywhere, they could learn the business of living in Canada admirably in the older provinces, and then, if they moved to the west, they would go as very desirable settlers. There is no part of Canada where an immigrant could learn the duties of Canadian citizenship better than in the older provinces, where all the machinery necessary to make him a thoroughly well qualified Canadian citizen exists in great perfection. In the older provinces of Canada, while we have not the great fertility that exists in the west we have a capacity for maintaining a large population. The little province of Prince Edward Island maintains by far the largest population per mile that is to be found in any part of Canada. It has a population of fifty to the square mile, and if the most desirable parts of Canada had an equal density of population. Canada would contain a population of 100,000,000. Prince Edward Island is an exceedingly prosperous part of Canada ; it is a very fertile and productive country, and is most important to Canada. It has not only great powers of production, but those powers are being developed, not in that wasteful fashion that prevails in the west, where the whole business of the farmer is to produce enormous quantities of grain and ship it out of the country as rapidly as possible. In Prince Edward Island, as well as in a great part of the older provinces, you do not have that process of producing grain in enormous quantities and exporting it in a very wasteful fashion. You have, on the other hand, an organized industry. That grain is a raw material which is converted,
through feeding, into butter, milk, cheese, pork and beef, and you have a condition of things far more valuable to the country in every respect than that in which we see the settler exhausting as rapidly as he can the fertility of his acres in order that he may export the grain he raises out of the country as rapidly as possible, and doing it all with the least expenditure of labour. In these eastern provinces we have conditions which make for the welfare of the country, and it would be to my mind most important that these older provinces should receive a large part of the care and interest of the government, and that as large a part as possible of the immigration to Canada should be turned into them and be induced to stay there as long as possible. I am pleased, of course, to note that at last we are beginning to receive a large increase in our immigration, and I am, to a certain extent, pleased to hear our friends from the west raise the note of warning against the admission into Canada of undesirable immigrants. I hope to hear from the Minister of the Interior that care is being taken to make use of the powers conferred upon his department by the legislation of this parliament to see that no undesirable immigrant is allowed to land in Canada, or, if he does, to see that he is deported. Great as Is our power of assimilation, we cannot afford to receive disease, or filth, or weak intellects, or paupers. The attention of the minister should be directed to a careful sorting over of the people brought into Canada under the policy of the government. It is very gratifying to us to notice and to record the fact that even as compared with the United States our immigration has assumed such large proportions. In Canada we received last year some 65,000 - immigrants, and the United States received something like 618,000. We have a population of about one-fifteenth that of the United States and are receiving immigrants to the extent of about one-ninth the number going to that country, so that towards Canada the emigration of the old world is being turned to an extent larger in proportion than to that country, which for the last fifty years or more has been the Mecca of every one who desired to improve his position by changing his country.

I thought we would have heard from the hon. the Minister of the Interior. But for some reason or other he is not disposed to defend his policy or explain the weak features of it or say anything regarding it.
I would have expected, after the arraignment of his policy by the hon. members for Alberta and Winnipeg, that he would have been disposed to say something in defence of the system of immigration which he has been conducting, and vigorously conducting, of late years. It has always seemed to me that we have erred very greatly with

regard to our immigration policy. I admit that it is desirable our country should lie filled up as rapidly as possible provided we get the right class to come to it, but I have always thought it much more important that we should use greater discrimination in our selection of immigrants than we have done in the past and be more anxious to have quality than quantity. We have a glorious heritage, but I regret that we are too anxious to fill it up rapidly as though it was utterly impossible ever to populate our immense prairies in the west. But while our fields appear to be illimitable, it will not be a great problem to till them up, considering the overflow of population from eastern and continental countries seeking new worlds and the seventy million people to the south of us. We should therefore guard against being too eager to gain population irrespective of quality. Through our desire to populate our country rapidly, we are too ready to welcome the riff raff of every country in the world. Such a policy is not the best for the people who inhabit Canada to-day, nor will it bring about the best conditions for those who succeed us. The indiscriminate immigration that we are having to-day is to my mind full of menace to our people. It is one of the greatest of dangers that confront us. We are importing the undesirable elements of Europe and continental countries-people who know nothing about our institutions, who are not in any way to the manor born, who are aliens to the conditions of Canadian or American life, who are inbued with Instincts and natures which have not in themselves any tendency to elevate humanity but rather to lower it in every particular. Yet such people are coming in by the hundred thousand, and every nation under the sun which desires to send its overflow to this country has our assistance. It does not matter whether these immigrants are diseased, or mentally or physically weak, they are welcome. Take the Doukhobors, we received them with open arms, just as we do the diseased or pauper classes who are bound to be a burden on our country. We count them all up and congratulate ourselves on their numbers and praise the government for the increase in immigration. We read week after week of such and such a steamer landing so many thousands in Halifax, and we do not ask who they are. We do not inquire whether they are physically, mentally or educationally suited to the country. Their elevation in the scale of morality or civilization appears to be a matter of indifference. We ask nothing of these important factors, but we say that the government are entitled to our thanks because two or three thousand of these Galicians or Doukhobors or Finns or Russian Jews or Poles or Mexicans have come to settle in Canada. Canada to-day is the dumping ground for the refuse of every country in the world. And the time will come, though

it may not appear imminent now. when the social problems of life will press as heavily on us as they are doing to-day on the people in European and continental countries, and when it will tax the energy, ingenuity,, intelligence, political astuteness and statesmanship of our people to provide some protection against the dangerous elements we are importing in such large numbers. The fear that our country will not be filled up soon enough is not well-founded. A comparison is usually made between our country and the western states, to show liow rapidly their country was filled up-and how slowly ours. There is no use making comparisons between the settling of our western country and the filling up of the western states because the cases are not parallel, and you cannot draw any fair deduction from a comparison between them. It was not to be expected that our western country should fill up anything like as quickly as did the western states. The United States had. in the first place, a population of fifty or sixty million people, from which its unoccupied western states could draw settlement. In the eastern portion of that country, the population was becoming too dense and had to seek ail outlet. The cities and towns and rural districts in the east were becoming overcrowded, and the surplus found a field for their energies in the attractive wheat fields of the west. It was therefore an easy matter to populate the western states, when they had these millions at home to draw from, besides the immigration from European and continental countries. Very naturally, with these sources from which to draw population, their country settled much more rapidly than ours. And because we have not been able to vie with them in rapidity of settlement, we are apt to think there is something wrong with the condition of our country or with the way in which we carry on our immigration. But I say that it is not a fair comparison, for they had fifty or sixty of millions of their own people to draw upon, while we had only three or four million. Many portions of their country were overcrowded while we were not overcrowded in any part of ours. Again, they had commerce in every part of the world, vessels going to all European countries, and naturally they would attract a larger number of people to their country than we would to ours. We were comparatively a home-staying people, having little commerce and littie communication with European continental countries, and so could not be expected to draw from them as the United States did. Then, the United States had plenty of money to spend in immigration. She could spend hundreds of dollars where we could only spend dollars, so that in this respect also she has a great advantage.
We are reasoning on the same lines, while all these conditions have changed. AYe stand at the beginning of this new century faced

by new conditions. The territory of the United States is crowded, and the people are looking for the virgin soil of new fields to settle upon, with conditions of climate, soil and institutions similar to their own. Therefore, we have now seventy-five millions of people to draw upon to fill up our country, whereas a few years ago the surplus population of the United States was settling in their own west. The advantages now offered by our country for a start in life are so much greater than those in any portion of the United States that, of necessity, the people must move to our country and settle here. We are glad to welcome these people, because we know they are very-similar to ourselves. They- are accustomed to the conditions of climate, soil and institutions of our country-, and they can, with a little change of habit take up the responsibilities of life with us. And they make perhaps, some of the best settlex-s we can get. But they- are coming whether we spend money among them or not. The land companies acting as immigration agents in St. Paul, Minneapolis, Dulxith, Chicago, Detroit and Cleveland, companies that buy-eighty, one hundred or two hundred thousand acres of land in Western Canada and sell it to the people of the United States through agencies in these great cities- these concerns have established themselves as immigration agents that are more profitable to us than any system of immigration that we can carry out in their country. That being the case, is it desix-able that we should keep an army of immigi-ation agents in the United States to-day ? We are told that we have 280 agents who are. working there upon commission and salai-y. If we were to dismiss every one of these but ten or twelve we should have plenty. And 1 believe we should have quite as many- immigrants as are coming in to-day. They are making money out of us, but there is no reason why we should spend money for this pui-pose, because the immigrants would come in in any- case. A few years ago we spent only $120,000 for immigration ; and the oppositon of that day declai-ed that this was too large an exepnditure. Last year we spent $560,000 and there is not half the need for the expenditure to-day that there was five, seven or ten years ago. Because of these other influences of which I have spoken which ai-e sure to have immigrants whether our expenditure be great or small. We will get the immigrants in any case
And keep them. We used to lose them.
And keep them. There is no trouble in keeping the great bulk of them.
There used to be.

Because we had not the conditions of life that we have to-day. As 207
we open up the country, build more railways, make the country more productive, and develop more manufacturing establishments that will give employment to people, there will be less trouble in keeping them. We are getting a very respectable class of people and we desire to get as many as we can of Irish, English, Scotch, Gex

man and French. All these we welcome because they make good and desirable immigrants. And I think we would be entitled to spend a reasonable amount of money to get a reasonable number of these people to come to our country. But we should exercise careful discrimination as to whom we allow to come in. I do not apprehend any danger from people of the races I have named, but I do appi-ehend danger from those coming from European continental countries where the degeneracy- of human life is greater than in the others. If we exercised wiser precaution we would exclude many- who now are allowed to come in. We find that last year we allowed to come in 3,934 paupers. I was struck with an experience I had a few weeks ago in Winnipeg. Three times in one day I was stopped in the stx-eets by beggars. Who were they ? Concerning two, I was told in most unmistakable way that they had landed in the country but lately and had nothing to live upon. I said :	' Why don't you go to work ? ' The
answer was :	' The work here is not such
as we have been accustomed to.' These are not the desirable class to have here. Then we admitted 704 diseased people. Have we not enough diseased at home, physically and mentally, persons who must remain foi-ever a burden upon the charity of oui* people, filling our hospitals and almshouses, that we should take them from European countries ? We are doing wx-ong in not exercising greater discx-imination in preventing this class of immigration. We find that the United, States rejected 4,534 from Canada and Mexico. What were they rejected for ? They seemed to be good enough for Canada, but the United States rejected thm. We were told the other day that w.e sent hack a few, but comparatively very few. There are a lax-ge number of these undesirable people in Canada to-day. We welcome people from England, fx-om Ireland, Scotland. Germany or France, because we know what they are. They belong to the races to which we belong, they axe men who will tend to the elevation of our population, and to the progress of our coxxn-try. They are accustomed to our institutions. they are suitable to our climate, and we desire to get them. But there are many immigrants coming from continental countries that we do not desire to get, that we woxxld be better without. Better a small population that are living under favourable conditions, that ax-e happy and contented, than a country filled up with paupers. We are often told that we want population. If



that is the great need to make a country great, go over to China and Japan and look at the conditions prevailing there-four) hundred and fifty millions of people, the great bulk of whom are living iu a condition worse than that of the brute beasts of our country, humanity almost too low to be called humanity, conditions of life below the lowest that prevail in our own country. Is that what you want to make of Canada. Is there nothing else to be desired but an immense population ? We must take into account how that population is employed, whether they are living in comfort, in contentment, whether they are educated. I say it is much better to be careful about the quality of our population; husband our broad acres for the overflow of our own country; be more careful about whom we allow to come in, and try to conduct the affairs of this country so that we may keep those who settle among us by affording them employment which will keep them happy and contented. In my judgment we need not incur a very heavy expenditure for immigration to-day, because we will get plenty of it whether we spend much or little. It is not the part of wisdom to send an army of immigration agents into foreign countries. We should be more careful to discriminate between those whom we allow to come into this country and those we keep out. Keep out those who are mentally and physically unsound and diseased. Above all things we should endeavour to keep that class of people out of our country. We have enough disease at home. The expenditure for immigration is entirely too -large, in my judgment, and might be greatly cut down.
Tnere is another thing to be regretted, and I have spoken of it before in this House. I have always regarded the custom of planting people in colonies as wrong. I think the immigrants should be mixed with our own people. We could teach them many things which it would be advantageous for them to know, but when ypu plant them in colonies they live according to the conditions of life at home, they are apt to keep all those habits which they brought with them from home and which might not be suitable for our country. We have not the opportunities of teaching them that we would have if they were mixed up with our own people. I believe there should be a fusion of races and population, and if we make a proper discrimination among those whom we allow to come here, the results cannot fail to be beneficial to Canada. We should never set apart so many townships for this colony and so many for that, so many for the Barr colony, or the Doukhobor colony, or the Galician colony, or the colony of Russian Jews. In my judgment that is wrong, and we will live to regret it. There is too much discrimination against our own Canadians. If we try to get people in from the United States, what do we do ? In the first place, we pay an agent a commission Mr. SPROULE.
to bring them here. Suppose that agent goes over there and tries to bring in a family composed of ten individuals. There is a father and five sons. We pay him $3 a piece as commission to bring them here. Then take the mother, we pay $2 to bring her here; then take the three children and we pay $1 each, that is $23 to bring that family over here. We give them a ticket which enables them to get a reduction in transportation of at least $10. That makes $33 as the cost of bringing that family over here. Now take a family from Ontario, or Quebec, or Nova Scotia, or New Brunswick, or Prince Edward Island, how much do we pay them V There is nothing for commission to get them to come. They desire to come, because they think they can better their situation. What assistance do we give them ? Not a dollar, but we give it to the foreigner. Therefore I say we are discriminating against our own people, who are the best people in the world that we could have to settle up that country. Again, we are sending out literature to ali the world to induce immigrants to come here, but our maps are made over in Chicago. We have not intelligence and brains enough in Canada to make a map, and so the Minister of the Interior must go over to the United States and pay them Canadian money to make maps for us, which ought to be made at home. I do not care if we paid half as much more on a home-made map, so long as we spent our money at home. Let us keep our money and our labour in our own country, for our own people, and not spend it abroad. In these lines I think our immigration policy is deficient, and the people of Canada will condemn the Minister of the Interior and the department over which he presides for the way this immigration business is carried on. In my judgment it is wrong in many respects, and the government are entitled to censure for the system with which they are conducting the immigration business of our country to-day. It ought to be amended, it cannot be changed one hour too soon; otherwise, in the near future there will rise up a sentiment which no government can withstand, and which will oblige the government to change their system much more rapidly than they desire.

I am sorry to say that I did not have the pleasure of listening to all the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Sproule), but I have heard enough of what he said, and of what has been said by other hon. gentleman on this question, to justify me in addressing the House for a few moments. The hon. gentleman has been discussing the question of the army of immigration agents that this government has employed at the present time in the United States. Now I want to say that from my knowledge of the army of immigration agents that have been employed in the United

States, we are getting satisfactory results. He says that some years ago when his friends were in power they spent $100,000 on immigration, but, he did not tell the House what we got for the expenditure of that $100,000. I know what we got in one instance. We got a few Jew pedlars that were brought up to that country. Talk about paupers ! I do not know what you would call them; they turned out to be criminals, because they were not long in the country before some of them were lauded in the jails in Calgary, Winnipeg and other portions of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories. As far as paupers are concerned my hon. friend said that he went to Winnipeg last year and that he saw a lot of paupers. He should hare gone west previous to 1896. As a matter of fact we were nearly all paupers before the people turned the hon. gentleman and his friends out of power. There was scarcely any one else in the North-west Territories, and it is too bad that the hon. gentleman did not come up about that time. He goes on to say that he does not believe in colonies. Who introduced the system of colonies? The hon. gentleman's friends, and he, himself. because he was a memb.er of the House at that time, first introduced the system of colonies, but the difference between their system of colonies and the system of this government is, that, whereas, every colony they established was starved out and the people had to leave, tire colonies that are being introduced now are thriving and successful. The Barr Colonists.
The Saskatchewan ' Herald ' of Battleford, the pioneer Conservative paper of the territories, in a recent issue pays a high tribute to the members of the colony promoted by Rev. I. M. Where a few weeks ago there stood a couple of hundred bell-shaped tents, containing part of the British colony, there are to-day less than a dozen, and within the past few days nearly all the remaining Britishers, who have for various reasons not located, are now on lands *which they have homesteaded. Probably the most striking feature of the whole movement is the degree of perseverance shown by the new settlers. howl went up against the Galicians, and I am sorry to say that my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) joined in it, but to-day there is no person in the west who will say a word against the Galicians. My hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson), who introduced this resolution, showed us a lot of papers, and he wished to lead the House to believe that we were wasting money in advertising.
